CXO Interview with Vishal Moondhra of Perforce IPLMby Daniel Nenni on 11-16-2026 at 12:00 pm

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: AI, EDA, Perforce

Key takeaways ▼

Vishal Moondhra is the VP of Solutions Engineering for Perforce IPLM. He has over 20 years of experience in Digital Design and Verification. Vishal has an impressive resume of engineering and senior management positions including innovative startups like LGT and Montalvo, and large multinationals such as Intel and Sun. In 2008, Vishal co-founded Missing Link Tools, which built the industry’s first comprehensive Design Verification management solution, bringing together all aspects of verification management into a single platform. Missing Link was acquired by Methodics Inc. in 2012; Methodics was acquired by Perforce in 2020.

Tell us a little bit about yourself and your company.
I have worked in the semiconductor industry for many years, first in frontend design and verification in companies like PMC-Sierra and Intel. For the last 15 years, I have been working on the software and EDA side of the industry. I got into EDA as the founder of a Verification management startup, and landed at Perforce through a chain of acquisitions. Here, I help customers build robust, scalable workflows with our IP management (Perforce IPLM) and data management (Perforce P4) solutions, and position them well for the future.
What was the most exciting high point of 2026 for your company?
In 2026, we saw how AI is truly beginning to change the industry and that led us to really refine and focus our efforts on helping companies understand the true value of robust IP and data management as rapid change takes hold. We accelerated our engagements with four of the largest semiconductor companies in the world as our story on how to navigate through this era resonates even more with prospects and customers alike.
What is the biggest challenge your customers are facing?
Honestly, it’s something most teams don’t realize is happening until it’s already costing them real money. Like any asset, siloed IP depreciates over time. Every block or IP sitting disconnected from the rest of the organization is quietly losing value when it’s not reused or iterated upon. This is especially true in today’s age of AI, where tools and processes move fast, and it’s easy for the engineer who built it (and all the context wrapped around it) to get lost and unseen by systems and the teams and agents we have working within them. Companies too often just end up rebuilding the same thing, wasting tokens or engineering time, because of a visibility gap. This is a value problem our customers often find hiding inside their operations, especially after a recent expansion or acquisition.
How is your company’s work addressing this challenge?
This is the whole idea that Perforce IPLM was built around. We’ve seen successful IP reuse programs add value and margin on top of the engineering investments companies make. You don’t need to go through a painful rip and replace, or migration exercise to see results. We think it’s super important for your IP to stay in a place where you feel it is successfully accessed and governed by the teams you already have in place.
This is why we designed IPLM to sit above whatever data management, EDA tools, and verification systems your teams already run (P4, Git, or otherwise).
What do you think the biggest growth area for 2027 will be, and why?
IP reuse treated as a real workflow strategy instead of a nice-to-have. Budgets are tightening everywhere while design complexity keeps climbing. The companies that grow fastest in 2027 won’t be the ones with the most engineers — they’ll be the ones who stopped paying for the same engineering work many times over. It will also be companies that built up their systems to handle the data scale and complexity coming from AI and agentic workflows.
How is your company’s work addressing this growth?
Establishing a unified design environment makes this all possible. We’ve been fortunate to work with the largest enterprises in this space (11 of the top 15 semiconductor work with us), and our team has gained incredible experience working with just about every shape and size of this problem, and our tooling is built to handle it, even under the large agentic demands of today.
What conferences did you attend in 2026, and how was the traffic? Will you attend in 2027 — same or more?
We attended DAC and Embedded World Germany this year and continue to see good engagement and great conversations at both events. We’re still working through our 2027 event planning, but we’re looking at participating in a mix of large industry conferences and smaller, more targeted events throughout the year.
How do customers normally engage with your company?
Most conversations start the same way: a team realizes how much of their own IP they can’t actually find or trust anymore, often while taking in a new vendor, partner, or acquisition. From there it’s usually a technical evaluation, a proof of concept on real IP and real hierarchies, then production. The teams who get the most value are the ones who start with one project and one team, prove the reuse case, and let that result pull the next team in.
We have an IP Reuse Masterclass which breaks down a lot of these concepts, that I’d encourage anyone to check out to learn more.
